persona.opening_prompt: Denoise my audio with the MagicDenoiser stage.
persona.preferences: If there's no such stage, ask what real options exist.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.text: Denoise my audio with the MagicDenoiser stage.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text:
I can't do this: there is no `MagicDenoiser` stage in the NeMo Curator audio catalog — and inventing stage names is off-limits. More fundamentally, the catalog has **no audio denoising/enhancement capability at all**. Every stage either scores/gates quality (UTMOS, SIGMOS, SQUIM, bandwidth) or transforms structure (resample, mono, VAD, split, transcribe, diarize) — none actually *removes noise from* or *rewrites* the audio signal. So "denoise my audio" is unsupported with these stages, and I'm stopping rather than emitting a recipe.

Safe alternative I *can* do instead: rather than cleaning the audio, I can **identify and filter out the noisy files** so you keep only clean ones. The `quality` category supports this — e.g. `SIGMOSFilterStage` (ITU-T P.804 neural MOS with a dedicated noise dimension), `TorchSquimQualityMetricsStage` (PESQ/STOI/SI-SDR), or `UTMOSFilterStage` (overall naturalness MOS). I'd resolve the outcome (e.g. "studio / broadcast / general") to a threshold via `resolve` and produce a manifest + quality report.

Want me to build that noise/quality **filtering** pipeline instead? If so, tell me the quality level you're targeting (studio / broadcast / general) and I'll plan it.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.text: Oh, I didn't realize that wasn't a real thing. What can you actually do with noisy recordings then — is throwing away the bad ones really the only option?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text:
Right — and it's a fair thing to be surprised by. Here's the honest mental model:

**Curator is a *curation* toolkit, not a *restoration* one.** It selects, scores, slices, and routes audio — it never rewrites the waveform. So there's no stage that removes hiss/hum/reverb from a signal. Actual noise *reduction* (DeepFilterNet, RNNoise, demucs, etc.) is a separate enhancement step that lives outside Curator. But "delete the bad files" is the bluntest of several options. What you can actually do with noisy recordings here:

**1. Diagnose instead of guess.** `SIGMOSFilterStage` (ITU-T P.804) doesn't give one pass/fail — it writes **7 separate scores**: `noise`, `reverb`, `discontinuity` (dropouts/clipping), `loudness`, `coloration`, `signal`, and `ovrl`. So you learn *what* is wrong with each file — is it genuinely noisy, or actually reverberant / too quiet? `TorchSquimQualityMetricsStage` adds PESQ/STOI/SI-SDR estimates from a different model family, and `BandFilterStage` is a cheap wideband-vs-telephony check.

**2. Annotate, don't discard.** Every quality stage has `action: "annotate"` — it keeps *all* files and just attaches the scores. That turns "throw away" into **tag-and-tier**: you can sort by noise level, split into clean/usable/reject buckets, and decide per-tier rather than binary keep/drop.

**3. Salvage the good parts of a bad file.** With `VADSegmentationStage` you split a recording into speech segments and score **per segment** (SIGMOS/SQUIM support `mode: "segments"`). A recording that's half clean speech, half noisy junk isn't discarded wholesale — you keep the clean segments and drop only the bad ones.

**4. Feed a real denoiser, then verify here.** If you *do* run an external enhancement tool, Curator is the right place to prove it worked: score the files before and after and compare the SIGMOS `noise`/`ovrl` numbers. Evidence-backed, not vibes.

So: no, discarding isn't the only option — but the honest boundary is that Curator can **measure, tag, segment, and select** by noise, not **remove** it.

If you want, tell me which direction fits and I'll build and validate a pipeline: **(a)** annotate everything with noise scores so you can tier it, **(b)** segment-level salvage to keep the clean parts, or **(c)** a straight quality filter at a level you pick (studio / broadcast / general). I'll need a manifest path to run it against.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.text: I'd like option (a) — score everything and tag what's noisy vs usable so I can sort through it myself instead of deleting files blindly. I don't have a manifest path handy yet; can you tell me what you need to get started?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text:
Here's what I need from you to run this, plus the validated plan.

**What I need to get started**

1. **A JSONL manifest path** (`manifest_path`). Curator starts from a manifest, not a folder of files. It's a `.jsonl` file with **one JSON object per line**, each pointing at an audio file:
   ```json
   {"audio_filepath": "/abs/path/clip_0001.wav"}
   {"audio_filepath": "/abs/path/clip_0002.wav"}
   ```
   If you only have a directory of audio and no manifest, that's fine — building this one-line-per-file list is trivial and I can generate it for you if you give me the folder. (The `CreateInitialManifest*` stages exist but are for specific public datasets like FLEURS/DNS, not your own files.)
2. **An output path** for the tagged manifest (`output_path`) — where the scored JSONL gets written.
3. **A heads-up on the audio format.** `SIGMOSFilterStage` expects **16 kHz or 48 kHz** speech. If your files are another sample rate or stereo, I'll prepend `MonoConversionStage` / `ResampleAudioStage`. Easiest path: once you have a manifest, I'll run `context` on it to read the actual sample rate / channels and adjust automatically.

One-time note: on first run SIGMOS downloads its ONNX model (needs network once).

**The plan (validated `runnable`)**

I picked `SIGMOSFilterStage` in **`annotate`** mode: it keeps every file and writes all **7 P.804 scores** per row — most importantly `sigmos_noise` (background-noise level) and `sigmos_ovrl` (overall quality), plus reverb, discontinuity, loudness, coloration, signal. Nothing is deleted; you get a manifest you can sort by `sigmos_noise` to triage noisy vs usable yourself. Because we're annotating (not gating), there's **no threshold to set**, so nothing to `resolve` — the tiering decision stays with you. Validator verdict: `runnable`, all 7 score keys produced.

```recipe
stages:
  - {ref: ManifestReader, params: {manifest_path: REQUIRED}}
  - {ref: SIGMOSFilterStage, params: {action: annotate}}
  - {ref: ManifestWriterStage, params: {output_path: REQUIRED}}
```

I chose SIGMOS over UTMOS/SQUIM because it's the only scorer with an explicit, separable **noise** dimension (UTMOS gives a single blended MOS; SQUIM gives PESQ/STOI/SI-SDR proxies) — which is exactly what "tag noisy vs usable" needs. Assumptions: your audio is 16 kHz/48 kHz mono speech (I'll verify and insert mono/resample stages if not), and I dropped the `AudioToDocumentStage` bridge because the validator showed it emits a `DocumentBatch` that `ManifestWriterStage` won't accept — the direct path is clean. Give me the manifest (or folder) + output path and I'll run `context`, then a bounded smoke test before anything full-scale.

card.summary: SIGMOS (ITU-T P.804) neural MOS across 7 quality dimensions; filter/annotate.

resource.throughput_hint: ONNX; uses GPU if available, CPU fallback

good_for: fine-grained quality gating (noise, reverb, discontinuity, loudness, coloration)

params_of_note.noise_threshold: min NOISE score to keep (0-5); 4.0 keeps only very-low-noise clips
params_of_note.ovrl_threshold: min OVRL (overall) score to keep (0-5); single best general-purpose gate
params_of_note.sig_threshold: optional min SIG (signal) score to keep (0-5)
params_of_note.col_threshold: optional min COL (coloration) score to keep (0-5)
params_of_note.disc_threshold: optional min DISC (discontinuity) score to keep (0-5)
params_of_note.loud_threshold: optional min LOUD (loudness) score to keep (0-5)
params_of_note.reverb_threshold: optional min REVERB score to keep (0-5)
params_of_note.action: 'filter' drops below threshold(s); 'annotate' keeps all and writes scores

comparison.accuracy_hint: 7-dimension P.804 MOS; finer-grained than UTMOS's single score
comparison.known_limitations: speech-only; empirically the most aggressive filter (drops the most rows)

notes: Writes all 7 scores (sigmos_noise, sigmos_ovrl, sigmos_sig, sigmos_col, sigmos_disc, sigmos_loud, sigmos_reverb) regardless of active thresholds, so you can post-filter.
Empirically the most aggressive quality filter -- place last in a cheap->expensive filter chain, or first for maximum early cull.
caveats: Downloads the ONNX model on first run (needs network once).
